questions.question: In 606 CE, **Harshavardhana** ascended the throne at Kannauj[cite: 3]. Which dynasty did he belong to[cite: 3]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 63)

options.explanation: Incorrect. Harsha belonged to the Pushyabhuti (or Vardhana) dynasty[cite: 3].
Correct. Harshavardhana belonged to the Pushyabhūti (or Vardhana) dynasty[cite: 3].
Incorrect. Pulakeshin II belonged to the Chalukyas[cite: 7, 16].
Incorrect. Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas[cite: 11].

questions.explanation: Harshavardhana belonged to the **Pushyabhūti** (or Vardhana) dynasty, whose earlier capital was Sthāneshvara[cite: 3].

questions.question: Which scholar and court poet patronised by Harsha wrote the biographical work *Harshacharita* and the novel *Kādambarī*[cite: 4, 5]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 4-5)

options.explanation: Incorrect. Ravikirti was the court poet of Pulakeshin II[cite: 16].
Incorrect. Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini[cite: 13].
Correct. Banabhatta composed Harshacharita and Kadambari[cite: 5].
Incorrect. Dandin was a poet hosted by the Pallavas[cite: 19].

questions.explanation: **Bāṇabhaṭṭa** (also known as Bāṇa) patronised by Harsha, wrote *Kādambarī* and the biography *Harshacharita*[cite: 4, 5].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim who travelled across India between 630 and 644 CE and took back over 600 Sanskrit manuscripts was ___[cite: 5].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 65)
questions.explanation: **Xuanzang** visited India between 630 and 644 CE during Harsha's reign and recorded comprehensive accounts of Indian polity and culture[cite: 5, 6].

questions.question: Harshavardhana's military advance south of the **Narmada River** was checked by which ruler[cite: 7]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 67)

options.explanation: Correct. Pulakeshin II of the Chalukya dynasty checked Harsha's southward advance[cite: 7].
Incorrect. Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas later in the 8th century[cite: 11].
Incorrect. Narasimhavarman I defeated Pulakeshin II[cite: 18].
Incorrect. Aditya I was a Chola ruler[cite: 19, 21].

questions.explanation: Harsha attempted to expand beyond the Narmada but was stopped by **Pulakeśhin II** of the Chalukya dynasty[cite: 7].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: King Harshavardhana held a grand charitable assembly every five years at ___, where he gave away much of his accumulated wealth[cite: 7].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 67)
questions.explanation: Harsha conducted a major assembly every five years at **Prayāga** (present-day Prayagraj) at the sacred confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna[cite: 7].

questions.question: Who was chosen by the people around 750 CE to bring stability to the Bengal region, establishing the **Pāla dynasty**[cite: 8]?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Dharmapala was Gopala's successor[cite: 8].
Correct. Gopala was chosen by the people around 750 CE[cite: 8].
Incorrect. King Bhoja was a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler[cite: 10].
Incorrect. Dantidurga established Rashtrakuta rule[cite: 11].

questions.explanation: **Gopāla** was chosen as ruler by the people in 750 CE to end disorder, laying the foundation of the Pala dynasty[cite: 8].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The ancient university of **Vikramaśhilā** on the banks of the Ganga was founded by the Pala emperor ___[cite: 8, 9].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'A university with scholars as gatekeepers' (Page 69)
questions.explanation: Emperor **Dharmapāla** founded the monastic university of Vikramaśhilā in the late 8th century[cite: 8, 9].

questions.question: At Vikramaśhilā University, prospective students were examined at the entrance by an official known as a[cite: 9]:
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'A university with scholars as gatekeepers' (Page 69)

options.explanation: Incorrect. Samanta refers to a vassal or subordinate feudatory[cite: 22].
Correct. A 'dvārapaṇḍita' was a scholar gatekeeper who tested students[cite: 9].
Incorrect. Yuvaraja means crown prince[cite: 26].
Incorrect. Goshthika was a temple council member[cite: 30].

questions.explanation: Each college at Vikramaśhilā had a **dvārapaṇḍita** ('scholar gatekeeper') who screened candidate admissions[cite: 9].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Gurjara-Pratīhāra dynasty was founded in the mid-8th century CE by ___[cite: 10].
questions.explanation: **Nāgabhaṭa I** founded the Gurjara-Pratīhāra dynasty and resisted Arab invasions into northwest India[cite: 10].

questions.question: Which prominent Gurjara-Pratīhāra king adopted the title **Ādi Varāha** and had coins struck with the boar incarnation of Vishnu[cite: 10]?

options.explanation: Incorrect. King Bhoja took the title of Adi Varaha[cite: 10].
Correct. King Bhoja was also designated Mihira and Adi Varaha[cite: 10].
Incorrect. Dantidurga was a Rashtrakuta king[cite: 11].
Incorrect. Lalitaditya was a Kashmiri ruler[cite: 13].

questions.explanation: **King Bhoja** (also known as Mihira) was a devotee of Vishnu and assumed the title **Ādi Varāha**[cite: 10].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The capital of the Rashtrakūṭa Empire was located at ___ (modern Malkheda in Karnataka)[cite: 11].
questions.explanation: The Rashtrakūṭas established their capital at **Mānyakheṭa** in Karnataka[cite: 11].

questions.question: The monolithic rock-cut **Kailashanātha Temple** at Ellora was commissioned by which Rashtrakūṭa ruler[cite: 11]?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Amoghavarsha I took the title Nripatunga[cite: 12].
Correct. Krishna I got the Kailashanatha rock-cut temple carved out at Ellora[cite: 11].
Incorrect. Dantidurga founded the dynasty[cite: 11].
Incorrect. Pulakeshin I was an early Chalukya ruler[cite: 16].

questions.explanation: Rashtrakūṭa king **Krishna I** commissioned the monumental monolithic Kailashanātha temple at Ellora[cite: 11].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Rashtrakūṭa monarch who ruled for 64 years and held the title 'Nripatunga' was ___[cite: 12].
questions.explanation: **Amoghavarsha I** adopted the epithet Nripatunga ('peak of kings') and reigned for 64 years[cite: 12].

questions.question: The historical chronicle *Rājataraṅgiṇī*, detailing the ruling dynasties of Kashmir, was written by[cite: 13]:

options.explanation: Correct. Kalhana authored the Rajatarangini in the 12th century[cite: 13].
Incorrect. Banabhatta authored the Harshacharita[cite: 5].
Incorrect. Abhinavagupta was a Kashmir Shaivism philosopher[cite: 15].
Incorrect. Brahmagupta was an astronomer and mathematician[cite: 28].

questions.explanation: **Kalhaṇa** composed the Sanskrit historical epic *Rājataraṅgiṇī* ('The River of Kings')[cite: 13].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: In 10th-century Kashmir, Queen ___ ruled firmly by forging strategic alliances and ruthlessly suppressing rivals[cite: 13].
questions.explanation: Queen **Diddā** consolidated control over 10th-century Kashmir, founding towns and building temples[cite: 13].

questions.question: The famous eulogy (*prashasti*) inscribed on the walls of the Meguti Jain temple at Aihole was composed by[cite: 16]:

options.explanation: Incorrect. Banabhatta was Harsha's court poet[cite: 4, 5].
Correct. Ravikirti was Pulakeshin II's court poet who wrote the inscription[cite: 16].
Incorrect. Dandin was patronised by the Pallavas[cite: 19].
Incorrect. Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini[cite: 13].

questions.explanation: Court poet **Ravikīrti** composed the Aihole inscription in Sanskrit celebrating Pulakeśhin II's military conquests[cite: 16, 17].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Pallava king Narasimhavarman I was known by the title ___, meaning 'wrestler' or 'warrior'[cite: 18].
questions.explanation: Narasimhavarman I held the title **Māmalla**, which commemorated his prowess as a warrior[cite: 18].

questions.question: Who revived the **Chola dynasty** in the 9th century and established Tanjāvūr as its capital[cite: 21]?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Aditya I was Vijayalaya's son who expanded the realm[cite: 21].
Correct. Vijayalaya restored Chola power in the 9th century[cite: 21].
Incorrect. Mahendravarman I was a Pallava king[cite: 18].
Incorrect. Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas[cite: 11].

questions.explanation: **Vijayālaya** revived Chola authority in the 9th century from his capital at Tanjāvūr[cite: 21].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Subordinate feudal rulers who administered territories and supplied military support to kings were called ___[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: Subordinate chieftains or tributaries who exercised regional authority were termed **sāmantas**[cite: 22].

questions.question: Detailed 10th-century inscriptions describing the democratic selection of members to the village council (*sabhā*) were discovered at[cite: 22]:

options.explanation: Correct. Uttaramerur inscriptions describe village council selection procedures[cite: 22].
Incorrect. Mamallapuram was known for rock-cut temples and ports[cite: 2, 18].
Incorrect. Malkheda (Manyakheta) was the Rashtrakuta capital[cite: 11].
Incorrect. Dashapura was the Aulikara capital[cite: 30].

questions.explanation: The Chola inscriptions at **Uttaramerur** explain the committee electoral rules of the local village *sabhā*[cite: 22].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: Scribes and administrative clerks who transitioned from an occupational category into a distinct jāti by the 10th century were the ___[cite: 25].
questions.explanation: The **Kāyasthas**, originally professional scribes and record keepers, formed a distinct endogamous jāti by the 10th century[cite: 25].

questions.question: In the South Indian Bhakti tradition, the 12 devotional poet-saints dedicated to Lord Vishnu were known as the[cite: 27]:

options.explanation: Incorrect. Nayanars were the 63 Shaivite poet-saints[cite: 27].
Correct. The 12 Alvars were devotees of Vishnu[cite: 27].
Incorrect. Dvarapanditas were university gatekeeper scholars[cite: 9].
Incorrect. Kayasthas were scribes and clerks[cite: 25].

questions.explanation: The 12 **Āḻvārs** were Tamil poet-saints dedicated to Vishnu, among whom the female saint Āṇḍāḷ was prominent[cite: 27].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The treatise *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta*, formulating foundational rules for operations with zero and negative numbers, was authored by ___[cite: 28].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'A galaxy of mathematicians and astronomers' (Page 88)
questions.explanation: **Brahmagupta** wrote the *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta* in 628 CE, laying principles of algebra and zero arithmetic[cite: 28].

questions.question: The invasion of the Hūṇas into central India in the 6th century was decisively crushed by the rulers of the[cite: 30]:

options.explanation: Correct. The Aulikaras of Dashapura defeated the Hunas[cite: 30].
Incorrect. Cholas ruled the deep South[cite: 21].
Incorrect. Palas ruled Bengal from the 8th century[cite: 8].
Incorrect. Pallavas were centred in Kanchipuram[cite: 18].

questions.explanation: King Yashodharma of the **Aulikara dynasty** (ruling from Daśhapura/Mandsaur) defeated the Hūṇa leaders[cite: 29, 30].

questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Arab commander who led the military campaign that conquered Debal and the province of Sindh in 712 CE was ___[cite: 3, 31].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Arabs arrive on India's shores' (Page 91)
questions.explanation: **Muhammad bin Qasim** conquered the port of Debal and defeated King Dāhar of Sindh in 712 CE[cite: 3, 31].

questions.question: Which ancient port located in southern Tamil Nadu handled maritime commerce with Southeast Asia for the **Pāṇḍya dynasty**[cite: 20]?

options.explanation: Incorrect. Thane is on the western coast[cite: 31].
Correct. Korkai was an active southern port of the Pandyas[cite: 20].
Incorrect. Debal was in the Indus delta[cite: 31].
Incorrect. Sthaneshvara was an inland northern capital[cite: 3].

questions.explanation: The Pāṇḍyas conducted brisk overseas maritime trade through their ancient seaport at **Korkai**[cite: 20].

questions.question: Explain the significance of the **Banskhera copper plate inscription** with respect to King Harshavardhana[cite: 4].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Great King of Kings' (Page 64)
questions.correctAnswer: The Banskhera copper plate inscription in Uttar Pradesh contains King Harsha's personal signature in Nagari script, which reads 'svahasto mama mahārājādhirāja śhrī harshasya' ('By my own hand, the great king of kings, Shri Harsha')[cite: 4]. It proves his direct administrative authority and reveals the evolution of the Nagari script[cite: 4].
questions.explanation: The Banskhera inscription features Harsha's royal endorsement and demonstrates script transitions preceding modern Devanagari[cite: 4].

questions.question: State two distinctive historical methods adopted by **Kalhaṇa** while compiling the *Rājataraṅgiṇī*[cite: 13].
questions.correctAnswer:
1. He examined eleven earlier historical chronicles composed by prior scholars to reconstruct past events[cite: 13].
2. He verified records against primary archaeological evidence, such as inscriptions on temple consecrations, land grants, and laudatory records[cite: 13].
questions.explanation: Kalhaṇa broke ground in Indian historiography by cross-referencing literary chronicles with epigraphic records without personal bias[cite: 13, 14].

questions.question: What core philosophy did **Ādi Śhaṅkarāchārya** propagate, and what was the strategic significance of the four *maṭhas* he established[cite: 14, 15]?
questions.correctAnswer: Ādi Śhaṅkarāchārya taught **Advaita Vedānta**, arguing that *Brahman* is the ultimate reality and the empirical world is *māyā* (illusion)[cite: 14, 15]. He established four *maṭhas* at the four corners of India (Badrinath, Puri, Dwarka, and Sringeri) to preserve Vedic learning and unify cultural traditions[cite: 15].
questions.explanation: Śhaṅkarāchārya formulated the philosophy of non-dualism and unified pan-Indian cultural and philosophical networks via his four monastic centres[cite: 14, 15].

questions.question: Highlight two key achievements of the Pallava king **Narasimhavarman I**[cite: 18].
questions.correctAnswer:
1. He defeated the Chalukya ruler Pulakeśhin II and captured the Chalukya capital at Badami (Vātāpi)[cite: 18].
2. He dispatched a successful naval expedition to Sri Lanka to help restore a Sinhalese prince to the throne[cite: 18].
questions.explanation: Narasimhavarman I 'Māmalla' expanded Pallava prestige by overcoming Badami and projecting naval strength into Sri Lanka[cite: 18].

questions.question: What information do **hero stones** (*vīragal*), like the one found at Eduthanur, provide about local village life and values[cite: 23]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'Trade, economy and urbanisation' (Page 83)
questions.correctAnswer: Hero stones commemorate individuals who sacrificed their lives defending local communities or livestock against cattle thieves and invaders[cite: 23]. For example, the Eduthanur stone honors both a village chieftain and his faithful dog who died defending local cattle[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Hero stones preserve local historical incidents, village security challenges, and communal ethics of valor and loyalty[cite: 23].

questions.question: Explain how the **Bhauma-Kara dynasty** of Odisha was exceptional regarding royal succession and political leadership[cite: 26].
questions.correctAnswer: While most Indian dynasties favored male heirs (*yuvarājas*), the Bhauma-Karas featured several reigning female sovereigns[cite: 26]. Queen **Tribhuvana Mahādevī I** consolidated the state, quelled rebellions, and assumed full imperial titles[cite: 26].
questions.explanation: The Bhauma-Karas stand out for recognizing queens as sovereign administrative and military leaders[cite: 26].

questions.question: How did the **Bhakti tradition** in South India challenge conventional social and gender boundaries[cite: 27, 28]?
questions.correctAnswer: The Bhakti tradition opened direct spiritual devotion to all individuals regardless of caste or gender, composing poetry in vernacular regional languages[cite: 28]. Several revered saints were Śhūdras, and women saints like **Āṇḍāḷ** and **Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār** were celebrated as major spiritual leaders[cite: 27, 28].
questions.explanation: South Indian Bhakti broke elite monopolies over worship by promoting egalitarian devotion across varied social groups[cite: 28].

questions.question: What distinct mathematical breakthrough is attributed to the 9th-century Jain scholar **Mahāvīra**[cite: 28, 29]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'A galaxy of mathematicians and astronomers' (Page 88-89)
questions.correctAnswer: Mahāvīra, who resided at the court of Rashtrakūṭa king Amoghavarsha, authored the first treatise on mathematics treated completely independent of astronomy[cite: 28, 29].
questions.explanation: Unlike contemporary astronomers who treated arithmetic strictly as a tool for planetary tracking, Mahāvīra established mathematics as an autonomous discipline[cite: 29].

questions.question: Describe two ways the **Hūṇas** assimilated into Indian society after their military defeats in the 6th century[cite: 30].
questions.correctAnswer:
1. They served as soldiers and joined local civic bodies, such as temple administrative councils (*goṣhṭhikas*)[cite: 30].
2. They adopted Sanskrit and Prakrit for inscriptions and issued coins bearing Indian royal titles and Hindu deities like Lakshmi, Shiva, and Vishnu[cite: 30].
questions.explanation: The nomadic Hūṇas integrated into Indian society by adopting local religious, administrative, and cultural practices[cite: 30].

questions.question: Why did the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712 CE result in a limited long-term political and religious transformation compared to Arab expansions elsewhere[cite: 32]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Arabs arrive on India's shores' (Page 92)
questions.correctAnswer: Indian rulers continuously resisted and pushed them back, restricting Arab rule to small pockets in Sindh and Punjab[cite: 32]. Consequently, the rulers abandoned iconoclasm and allowed Hindus and Buddhists to retain and rebuild temples, and keep priests in revenue sharing[cite: 32].
questions.explanation: Persistent military pushback by Indian dynasties forced Arab rulers to abandon mass replacement of regional social and religious structures[cite: 32].

questions.question: Match each **dynasty** in Column A with its primary **capital city** in Column B[cite: 11, 16, 18, 21].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: Map Fig. 3.16 and 'Further South' (Page 76-81)
questions.explanation: The Rashtrakūṭas ruled from Mānyakheṭa[cite: 11], the Pallavas from Kānchī[cite: 18], the early Chalukyas from Vātāpi[cite: 16], and the revived Cholas from Tanjāvūr[cite: 21].

questions.question: Match the ancient **author or scholar** in Column A with their **work or accomplishment** in Column B[cite: 5, 13, 16, 28].
questions.hint: Refer to Sections on Literature and Science (Pages 65, 73, 76, 88)
questions.explanation: Bāṇa wrote Harshacharita[cite: 5], Kalhaṇa composed Rājatarangiṇī[cite: 13], Ravikīrti authored the Aihole inscription[cite: 16], and Brahmagupta wrote the Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta[cite: 28].

questions.question: Match each **historical founder/ruler** in Column A with their associated **dynasty** in Column B[cite: 8, 10, 11, 16].
questions.hint: Refer to Sections on Chief Dynasties (Pages 68-76)
questions.explanation: Gopāla founded the Pāla dynasty[cite: 8], Nāgabhaṭa I founded the Gurjara-Pratīhāras[cite: 10], Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakūṭas[cite: 11], and Pulakeśhin I founded the Chalukyas[cite: 16].

questions.question: Match the famous **monument or sculpture** in Column A with its **associated region or dynasty** in Column B[cite: 2, 11, 21, 27].
questions.hint: Refer to Figures across the chapter (Pages 61, 71, 81, 87)
questions.explanation: Shore Temple was built by Pallavas[cite: 2], Kailashanatha by Rashtrakūṭas[cite: 11], Bahubali is at Shravanabelagola[cite: 27], and Nataraja bronzes flourished under Cholas[cite: 21].

questions.question: Analyze the causes, participants, and long-term consequences of the **Tripartite Struggle** over Kannauj[cite: 7, 8, 10].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'A Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj' (Pages 67-68)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Parties**: The contest involved the **Pālas** of eastern India, the **Gurjara-Pratīhāras** of western India, and the **Rashtrakūṭas** of the Deccan[cite: 7, 8].
2. **Causes**: Kannauj, located strategically in the fertile central Gangetic plain, was the symbol of imperial sovereignty across northern India after Harsha[cite: 7, 10, 12].
3. **Consequences**: Centuries of warfare depleted military resources, brought fluctuating fortunes with no permanent victor, and ultimately exhausted all three dynasties[cite: 8, 10].
questions.explanation: The Tripartite Struggle centered on dominance over Kannauj and weakened the three major early medieval Indian empires[cite: 7, 8, 10].

questions.question: How did the widespread practice of **royal land grants** transform rural agriculture and social structures between the 6th and 10th centuries[cite: 23]?
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'Trade, economy and urbanisation' (Page 83)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Expansion of Cultivation**: Kings, royal families, and vassals granted unused or forest land to individuals and religious institutions, bringing virgin land under active farming[cite: 23].
2. **Emergence of Intermediaries**: It created a landed class that did not cultivate the land directly, leading to non-cultivating intermediaries who collected revenue from peasant cultivators[cite: 23].
3. **Agricultural Infrastructure**: Beneficiaries and rulers invested in water harvesting systems, including extensive tanks and wells that boosted cash crop yields[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Land grants extended cultivation into forest fringes but created hierarchical agrarian relations between landlords and peasantry[cite: 23].

questions.question: Examine how India operated as an **international maritime hub** between the 6th and 10th centuries, identifying its key trading partners and commodities[cite: 18, 23, 24].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'Trade, economy and urbanisation' (Pages 83-84)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Western Trade Networks**: Indian ports on the western coast traded actively with Iran, Iraq, the Arabian peninsula, and East Africa using monsoon winds[cite: 23, 33].
2. **Eastern Maritime Trade**: Eastern ports under the Pallavas, Cholas, and Palas sailed to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and Chinese ports[cite: 8, 18, 23].
3. **Commodities and Cosmopolitan Presence**: India exported fine textiles (such as silk), spices, and ivory[cite: 18]. Copper-plate records confirm that communities of Christian, Muslim, and Jewish merchants lived and traded on India's coasts[cite: 24].
questions.explanation: India served as an oceanic commercial crossroad linking West Asian, African, and East Asian trade networks[cite: 23, 24, 33].

questions.question: Examine the role of **sāmantas** in medieval governance, outlining their administrative duties, military responsibilities, and risks to royal authority[cite: 22].
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Duties**: Sāmantas were subordinate vassals who administered outlying provinces and maintained local order on behalf of the monarch[cite: 22].
2. **Military Support**: They maintained troops and provided armed levies during royal military campaigns[cite: 22].
3. **Political Instability**: When central control weakened, ambitious sāmantas rebelled to declare independence, as seen when the Rashtrakūṭas overthrew their Chalukya overlords[cite: 22].
questions.explanation: The sāmanta mechanism decentralized territorial governance but created chronic structural instability at the central imperial level[cite: 22].

questions.question: Illustrate how early medieval rulers demonstrated **religious tolerance and pluralism**, citing examples from Harsha, the Palas, and the Rashtrakūṭas[cite: 5, 9, 11, 12].
questions.hint: Refer to Sections: 'The Palas', 'The Rashtrakūtas', and Cultural Life (Pages 65, 69, 71, 72)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Harsha**: Revered Lord Shiva while actively supporting Buddhism and organizing assemblies open to all faiths[cite: 5, 7].
2. **Pālas**: Though great champions of Mahāyāna Buddhism, many Pala rulers and successors patronized Shaivite temples and appointed Brahmin ministers[cite: 8, 9].
3. **Rashtrakūṭas**: Kings like Amoghavarsha embraced Jainism while funding Hindu temples[cite: 12]. Arab chronicles by Al-Mas'ūdī note that Muslim traders in Rashtrakūṭa territories were protected and allowed to build congregational mosques[cite: 12].
questions.explanation: Rulers patronized multiple religious traditions simultaneously, reflecting open philosophical and religious interaction[cite: 9, 11, 12].

questions.question: Detail the cultural and intellectual transmission between **India and the Arab world** in science and mathematics during the 8th and 9th centuries[cite: 28, 33].
questions.hint: Refer to Section: 'The Arabs arrive on India's shores' (Pages 92-93)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Translation of Sanskrit Treatises**: Sanskrit works on astronomy, medicine, and mathematics—notably Brahmagupta's *Brahmasphuṭasiddhānta*—were translated into Arabic in cultural centers like Baghdad[cite: 28, 33].
2. **Decimal Numerals and Zero**: The Arab world adopted the Indian decimal numeral system along with zero, openly acknowledging its Indian origin[cite: 33].
3. **Transmission to Europe**: These concepts later traveled to Europe through Arabic works, becoming internationally known as Hindu-Arabic numerals[cite: 33].
questions.explanation: Medieval Indian mathematical discoveries were assimilated through Baghdad's translation bureaus and revolutionized global science[cite: 33].

questions.question: Explain the dual reality of **social mobility and caste rigidity** in Indian society between the 6th and 10th centuries[cite: 24, 25].
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Flexibility & Mobility**: Occupational groups and dynasties rose in the hierarchy; lineages originating from Śhūdra backgrounds (such as the early Pālas) attained Kshatriya status through military conquest[cite: 25]. Professional scribes merged to form the Kāyastha jāti[cite: 25].
2. **Rigidity & Marginalisation**: Endogamy hardened, and discriminatory terms like *aspṛśya* ('untouchable') entered textual records[cite: 24, 25].
3. **Segregation**: Pilgrims like Xuanzang recorded that communities of scavengers, butchers, and executioners were forced to reside outside town walls[cite: 25].
questions.explanation: The varṇa-jāti system showed flexibility at the ruling elite level while hardening exclusion toward marginalized communities[cite: 25].

questions.question: Compare the nature and lasting impact of the **Hūṇa invasions** with the **early Arab invasions** of India[cite: 30, 31, 32].
questions.hint: Refer to Sections: 'The Hūṇas' challenge' and 'The Arabs arrive...' (Pages 90-92)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Aims & Origins**: The nomadic Hūṇas came from Central Asia as conquerors who settled within the land[cite: 30]. The Arabs swept across Sind motivated by imperial conquest and religious expansion from the caliphate[cite: 31].
2. **Assimilation vs Retention**: The Hūṇas completely absorbed into Indian society, adopting Indian religions, names, scripts, and military roles[cite: 30]. The Arabs maintained distinct cultural and political ties with the Islamic caliphate[cite: 31, 32].
3. **Resistance & Scope**: Both faced stiff regional resistance—the Hūṇas by the Aulikaras, and the Arabs by the Gurjara-Pratīhāras and Kashmiri kings—limiting their territorial sway[cite: 30, 32].
questions.explanation: Hūṇa invaders assimilated entirely into Hindu and regional society, whereas Arab campaigns established distinct frontier enclaves[cite: 30, 32].

questions.question: How did the valley of **Kashmir** function as an intellectual bridge linking northern India, Tibet, and Central Asia[cite: 15]?
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Sanskrit and Philosophical Center**: Kashmir was a leading center of Sanskrit scholarship and developed Kashmir Shaivism, producing polymaths like Abhinavagupta[cite: 15].
2. **Buddhist Conduit**: Monks, scholars, and sacred texts traveled between mainland Indian centers and Himalayan passes into Central Asia and Tibet[cite: 15].
3. **Artistic Excellence**: Kashmiri artisans, sculptors, and manuscript illustrators were actively sought after across northern India, the Himalayas, and Central Asia[cite: 15].
questions.explanation: Kashmir functioned as an intellectual hub connecting Indian philosophical traditions with Central Asian and Tibetan scholarship[cite: 15].

questions.question: Describe the architectural and sculptural innovations of the **Pallavas** and **Cholas** in Tamil Nadu[cite: 2, 18, 19, 21].
questions.hint: Refer to Sections: 'The Pallavas' and 'Further South' (Pages 61, 78, 81)
questions.correctAnswer:
1. **Pallava Rock Architecture**: Pioneered monolithic rock-cut cave temples and freestanding monolithic shrines (*rathas*) at Mamallapuram, along with structural stone temples like the Shore Temple[cite: 2, 18].
2. **Dynamic Relief Sculptures**: Sculpted expressive narrative reliefs in granite, such as Durga slaying Mahiṣhāsura and Mahābhārata tableaux[cite: 18, 19].
3. **Chola Grandeur and Bronze Casting**: Constructed vast structural stone temples and perfected lost-wax bronze casting, producing iconic masterpieces such as the dancing Shiva as **Naṭarāja**[cite: 21].
questions.explanation: Pallava rock-cut experiments established the base from which Chola structural architecture and bronze casting reached classical heights[cite: 18, 21].
